His breathing was still shallow, but steadier than it had been, and a faint flush of colour touched his cheek. She had been coaxing him through another fitful night, reading aloud from a book of travel tales until her voice was a mere whisper. Julian stirred, his eyes opening slowly. “You’re still here,” he murmured, a hint of his old mischievous smile playing about his lips. “I had a dream you had vanished, quite suddenly, into thin air. A frightful thought, as it meant I would have had to make my own tea.”

She managed a tired smile in return. “No such luck, I’m afraid. Though I confess the thought of a good cup of tea at this hour is rather tempting.” Her hand went to her brow, pushing back a stray wisp of hair. It was then she heard the sound of a carriage on the gravel drive, and a moment later, a firm, decisive knock at the front door. Her heart gave a sudden, unwelcome lurch. It could only be Arthur. He had promised to call today, and his promises, like his presence, were always unyielding.

She stood, stretching muscles stiff from the long vigil, and went to answer the door. Arthur stood upon the step, his formidable presence filling the doorway. His gaze swept over her, taking in her rumpled dress, the shadows beneath her eyes, the faint tremor in her hands which she clasped before her. “Eleanor,” he said, his voice deep and calm. “You look utterly spent.”

“I am merely a little tired, Arthur,” she replied, attempting a lightness she did not feel. “Julian has had another restless night. Do come in.”

He stepped past her, shedding his coat with a practiced movement, and she followed him into the sitting-room. The fire, which Thomas, the new house-boy, had attempted to light that morning, was a sorry spectacle of smouldering wood and acrid smoke. Arthur regarded it for a moment, his brows drawn in a slight frown. “Has no one tended to this?” he asked, a quiet note of disapproval in his tone.

“Thomas has been doing his best,” Eleanor said quickly, though her patience with Thomas’s efforts was wearing thin. “He means well, but he is rather clumsy.”

Arthur did not respond immediately. He went to the fireplace, surveying the pathetic heap. “Thomas,” he called, his voice carrying with an authority that Eleanor had never quite managed to master herself. “Thomas, come here at once!”

A moment later, Thomas appeared, his eyes wide and rolling as if already anticipating a lecture. His smile, when it came, was a vast, almost unnatural expanse across his dark face, a nervous reflex that always bewildered Eleanor. Arthur, however, seemed impervious to it. “You have made a mess of this, boy,” he stated, pointing to the smoking embers. “Fetch more kindling. And mind you do not make a spectacle of yourself.”

Thomas, after a dramatic nod, shuffled off to obey, his feet scraping loudly on the polished floor. Julian, hearing the commotion, called faintly from his room. “Is that Arthur? Tell him to come and amuse me, Eleanor!”

Eleanor sighed, a sound that was lost in the sudden crackle and roar of the fire as Arthur, with a few expert prods and shifts, brought it back to life. He turned to her, his expression serious. “You cannot go on like this, Eleanor. You are not yourself. Your face is pale, and you move as though every step is an effort.”

“Julian needs me,” she countered, her voice low. “His fever returns with such ferocity; I cannot leave him.”

“He is improving now,” Arthur said, his tone matter-of-fact. “I saw him for myself just now. He is weak, yes, but no longer in any danger. He is merely accustomed to your constant presence.”

“That is unkind, Arthur,” she said, her cheeks colouring slightly.

“Perhaps,” he conceded, his eyes holding hers. “But it is true. You have devoted yourself to him utterly, and he has taken advantage of it, however unconsciously. He has used your strength, and left you with none.”

She looked away, her lip trembling. “He has been so ill,” she whispered. “I could not abandon him. You know what he was like before; the doctors had all but given up hope.”

Arthur moved closer, standing very near to her. “And now he is well again,” he said, his voice softening, though the underlying resolve remained. “Is it not time you thought of yourself? Is it not time to replenish your own spirit?”

She turned to face him then, her eyes troubled. “What are you suggesting, Arthur?”

He took her hands in his, his touch firm and warm. “I am suggesting that you ride with me today. Away from this house, away from Julian’s demands, if only for a few hours. We could visit the Maxwells, or simply ride into the hills. It would do you good.”

“But Julian,” she began, pulling her hands gently from his grasp.

“Julian will be perfectly safe with Thomas, who, despite his clumsiness, is loyal enough,” Arthur interrupted, his voice edged with a new imperiousness. “Or, if you prefer, I shall send for Mrs. Davies from the village. But you, Eleanor, are coming with me.”

She hesitated, her gaze falling to the floor. She wanted to refuse him, to insist upon her duty, yet the thought of escaping, even for a brief time, was terribly alluring. But she felt a prickle of guilt, a sense of betrayal. “I cannot, Arthur,” she said, her voice barely audible. “It would not be right.”

He stood for a moment, observing her, his silence more potent than any argument. Then he reached out and gently lifted her chin, forcing her to meet his unwavering gaze. “Eleanor,” he said, his voice deep, persuasive. “When will you learn that your own well-being is not a luxury, but a necessity? I wish you to come.”

Her breath caught in her throat. The command in his voice, the directness of his eyes, the weight of his unspoken feelings, all combined to overwhelm her. She had been fighting for so long, and suddenly, the desire to surrender, to lean upon his strength, was almost unbearable. “Your wishes,” she said, her voice faltering slightly, “they always count with me, Arthur. You know they do. But I feel as though I am deserting him.”

“You are merely allowing him to stand on his own two feet for a change,” Arthur corrected, a faint smile touching his lips. “Come. Go and change into something suitable. I shall see to Julian.”

She looked at him for a long moment, a strange mixture of relief and trepidation filling her. He had a way of cutting through her objections, of taking control without asking. And though she felt a vague unease, a part of her was profoundly grateful. She nodded slowly. “Very well, Arthur,” she said, her shoulders slumping slightly in defeat, or perhaps, in sudden, unexpected peace. “I will come.”
